title: As Close to Carbyne As We're Probably Going to Get
body_text: Last year I wrote about the problems in generating carbyne, which is a (hypothetical) allotrope of carbon that is made up of rods of conjugated CC triple bonds, one acetylene stuck end-to-end with another and stretching off into the distance. Smaller versions of these structures have been made, and the outlook from those is not encouraging: as mentioned in that post, these are not very stable and get less stable as the chains get longer. Given that, it’s hard to imagine “bulk carbyne” really existing, and the reports of it over the years have (to the best of my knowledge) all been shown to be incorrect. This new preprint from a multicenter team, though, may be a close as we’re going to get. The instability of those “small carbyne” isomers seems to be through sudden exothermic crosslinking reactions, so what if you somehow wall things off? There have been reports (referenced in that link) of extended carbyne chains that are grown within carbon nanotubes. These are interesting, but the interactions with the walls of the tubes are very strong and the measured properties of the material show it to be pretty far off what you’d expect from a “real” carbyne chain. In this new work, such chains are confined in boron nitride nanotubes, and this material seems to make a much less intrusive package for it. These BNNTs don’t have the delocalized pi-electron cloud that you get with carbon nanotubes (which are essentially curled graphite) and they are electronically neutral. Not much, though, has been confined in these systems so far (some dye molecules and some stretches of graphene ribbon, as far as anyone can see). In this work, the authors take some short carbyne-ish chains (up to about ten carbons) and encapsulate then in a solution of boron nitride nanotubes, and then anneal them at high temperature. A similar process was used to produce carbyne chains inside carbon nanotubes in the earlier work mentioned above. This time, though, the properties of the “carbyne@BNNT” are quite different from the carbon nanotube-encapsulated material. Detailed Raman vibrational spectroscopy tells the tail - the experimental values land quite close to theoretical predictions for long-chain carbynes (which is not the case with the carbon nanotube material) and strongly suggest a symmetrical one-dimensional chain structure. The values for bond length alternation (BLA) are about tenfold tighter in this new material, and the carbyne@BNNT shows no photoluminescence at all, which is also consistent with theory. All in all, the authors conclude, this is about as close to “ideal carbyne” as we are likely to get! And the only way to realize this is with the most nonreactive, non-interacting confinement available. Carbyne chains of these lengths would surely rip themselves to pieces otherwise; the key is to not give them a chance.
